latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Circulating pathogenic Leptospira spirochetes during the first (septicemic) week, disseminating from skin/mucosal entry through blood to liver, kidney, lung, heart, eye, and CSF. This is the upstream substrate for nearly all downstream organ injury and the principal target of antibiotics.

Direct spirochete adhesion plus outer-membrane lipoprotein and LPS-like activation injure capillary endothelium, producing diffuse increased vascular permeability, conjunctival suffusion, petechiae, and a vasculitis-like leak that underlies multi-organ involvement and Weil syndrome severity.

Disorganization of hepatocyte intercellular junctions and canalicular bile transport with relatively little hepatocyte necrosis. Produces marked direct (conjugated) hyperbilirubinemia disproportionate to only mild–moderate AST/ALT elevation, the hepatic signature of Weil disease.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Leptospiral tubulointerstitial nephritis with distal tubular dysfunction
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Spirochete invasion of proximal and distal tubules with interstitial inflammation. Characteristic pattern is non-oliguric AKI in early phase with hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia (impaired Na/K reabsorption and increased distal K+ secretion), progressing to oliguric AKI with rising creatinine in severe disease.

Diffuse alveolar capillary injury with intra-alveolar hemorrhage, often preceding overt hemoptysis. Pathologic hallmark is linear immunoglobulin and complement deposition along alveolar basement membrane. Drives Severe Pulmonary Hemorrhage Syndrome (SPHS), the leading cause of death in modern series.

Interstitial myocarditis with lymphocytic infiltration and small-vessel vasculitis producing troponin rise, repolarization changes, atrial fibrillation, AV block, and occasionally cardiogenic shock; an under-recognized contributor to severe-disease mortality.

Multifactorial platelet drop driven by endothelial activation, platelet consumption at injured capillaries, marrow suppression, and immune-mediated clearance. Independent of overt DIC in most cases (fibrinogen often preserved) but strongly correlates with bleeding and mortality.

Direct spirochete invasion plus inflammatory injury of striated muscle, classically prominent in gastrocnemius. Manifests as severe calf tenderness/myalgia with elevated CK; a specific clinical clue and minor contributor to renal injury via pigment nephropathy.

Antibody-mediated clearance phase beginning around day 7. Coincides with reappearance of fever, aseptic meningitis, uveitis, and peak of immune-complex–driven organ inflammation. Time anchor for biphasic clinical pattern even when severe and septicemic phases overlap.

Leptospiral lipoprotein and atypical LPS engage TLR2/TLR4 producing high-grade fever, rigors, headache, myalgia, leukocytosis with left shift, marked CRP rise, and a sepsis-like syndrome. Drives the systemic inflammatory backbone of the leptospiremic phase.

Acute pyrogenic cytokine surge within hours of bactericidal antibiotic initiation due to release of spirochetal components. Produces transient fever spike, rigors, hypotension, and tachycardia; less common and milder than in syphilis/relapsing fever but clinically important to recognize.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Bacteremic spirochete load drives TLR2/TLR4-mediated innate cytokine activation responsible for fever, rigors, and sepsis-like presentation.
Spirochete adhesion to endothelium and outer-membrane–driven complement activation produce diffuse capillary leak that becomes the substrate of multi-organ injury.

Spirochete entry into hepatic sinusoids and hepatocytes disrupts canalicular bile transport and intercellular junctions, producing marked conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with disproportionately mild transaminase elevation.
Renal tubular invasion by leptospires is among the earliest tissue events; explains characteristic non-oliguric AKI with hypokalemia early, before frank renal failure develops.
Direct spirochete invasion of striated muscle, with characteristic gastrocnemius predominance, explains severe calf myalgia and CK elevation.
Generalized small-vessel endothelial injury localizes to alveolar capillaries with linear immunoglobulin/complement deposition, producing intra-alveolar hemorrhage that may precede overt hemoptysis.
Endothelial injury drives platelet adhesion, consumption, and immune-mediated clearance independent of overt DIC, explaining thrombocytopenia despite often-preserved fibrinogen.
Coronary microvascular injury and interstitial inflammation produce myocarditis with troponin rise and arrhythmia.
Specific antibodies clear circulating spirochetes from blood and CSF, terminating the leptospiremic phase around day 7.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: severe forms with high antibody-mediated alveolar damage
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Immune-complex and antibody deposition on alveolar basement membrane during the immune phase contributes to severe pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome.
Cytokine surge produces high fever (often 39–40 °C) with rigors, classically biphasic with a brief defervescence around day 7 and recurrence in the immune phase.
Severe frontal/retro-orbital headache is among the most consistent symptoms.
Marked acute-phase response with CRP often >100 mg/L during the leptospiremic phase.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: neutrophilic leukocytosis with left shift; may be normal or low in mild disease
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Neutrophilic leukocytosis with bandemia is typical and helps distinguish from many viral mimics (dengue, viral hepatitis).
Left shift commonly accompanies leukocytosis.
Procalcitonin rises in keeping with bacterial infection, supporting bacterial over viral cause when differentiating from dengue.
Conjunctival suffusion (bilateral redness without exudate) is a near-specific clinical sign reflecting conjunctival small-vessel injury.
Severe myalgia with characteristic gastrocnemius (calf) tenderness is a specific clinical clue.
CK is commonly elevated (often 5–50× upper normal) and helps separate from viral hepatitis and dengue when bilirubin is also elevated.
Marked hyperbilirubinemia, classically reaching 20–40 mg/dL in Weil disease, dominated by the conjugated fraction.
Predominantly conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia is characteristic.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: ALT typically only 2–5× upper normal, rarely >500 U/L
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Mild–moderate ALT/AST elevation disproportionately small versus bilirubin distinguishes from viral hepatitis.
Modestly elevated, often less than ALT in pure hepatic pattern; can be amplified by rhabdomyolysis-derived AST.
Mild–moderate ALP rise consistent with cholestatic pattern.
Rising creatinine reflects progression from non-oliguric tubulointerstitial injury to overt AKI in severe disease.
BUN rises with renal dysfunction, may be disproportionately high if volume-depleted.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: characteristic in non-oliguric early phase; reverses to hyperkalemia once oliguric AKI develops
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Distal tubular dysfunction with kaliuresis produces hypokalemia early, a fairly specific feature of leptospiral AKI versus other septic AKIs.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: occurs as injury progresses; many patients remain non-oliguric until late
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Severe nephritis with tubular obstruction and ischemia produces oliguria, marker of severity and dialysis need.
Direct interstitial nephritis is the dominant driver of AKI in leptospirosis, augmented by hypovolemia, sepsis, jaundice (cholemic nephrosis), and pigment from rhabdomyolysis.
Frank hemoptysis is a late, ominous manifestation; alveolar hemorrhage often precedes it.
Bilateral patchy alveolar opacities reflect alveolar hemorrhage rather than bacterial pneumonia.
Alveolar hemorrhage produces shunt physiology and hypoxemia.
Tachypnea precedes overt hypoxemia in SPHS and is an early warning sign.
Direct mechanistic driver of severe pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome (SPHS), the leading cause of leptospirosis mortality in modern series.
Diffuse alveolar damage and hemorrhage transition to ARDS physiology.
Thrombocytopenia (often 30–100×10^9/L, sometimes lower) commonly accompanies severe disease and is an independent predictor of bleeding and mortality.
Cutaneous petechiae and conjunctival hemorrhages reflect combined endothelial injury and thrombocytopenia.
Mucosal, gastrointestinal, and pulmonary bleeding correlates with platelet nadir.
Troponin elevation reflects myocarditis and is a poor-prognosis marker.
Direct contributor to arrhythmia, conduction block, and cardiogenic shock in severe disease.
Lymphocytic CSF pleocytosis with mildly elevated protein and normal glucose typifies the second-phase aseptic meningitis.
Specific IgM becomes detectable from approximately day 5–7, dominating diagnostic yield in immune phase. False negatives are common in the first 5 days.
Microscopic agglutination test rises with paired sera; fourfold rise or single titer ≥1:800 is diagnostic.
Blood PCR has highest sensitivity in the first 7 days when serology is still negative; sensitivity drops sharply after day 7.
Urinary shedding rises in second week; complements blood PCR for diagnostic window coverage.
Visible scleral and skin icterus, often with greenish tint due to high conjugated bilirubin in Weil disease.
Severe AKI requiring dialysis is a leading mortality contributor; early initiation of renal replacement reduces mortality.
Severe pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome carries case-fatality often >50% even with intensive support and is the leading direct cause of death.
ARDS independent of overt hemorrhage adds substantial mortality risk.
Cardiogenic shock and malignant arrhythmias from myocarditis contribute to severe-case mortality.
Distributive shock from endothelial leak and cytokine activation independently predicts death.
Bilirubin >20 mg/dL is an independent mortality predictor; jaundice marks Weil syndrome severity.
Capillary leak with hypovolemia and vasodilation produce hypotension.
Diffuse endothelial leak drives distributive shock physiology.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: within hours of first bactericidal antibiotic dose
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Pyrogenic surge transiently raises temperature and worsens rigors and tachycardia after antibiotic initiation.
Transient hypotension may complicate the cytokine surge after antibiotic initiation; usually self-limited within 24 h.

axes.shape_free_text: Abrupt onset high fever 38.5–40 °C within 1–2 days of incubation, classically biphasic with brief defervescence near day 7 and second peak in immune phase.
axes.second_peak: day 8–14 with immune phase, often with aseptic meningitis or uveitis

axes.shape_free_text: Tachycardia tracks fever and hypovolemia; persistent tachycardia after defervescence raises concern for myocarditis or hemorrhage.
Mildly elevated early; abrupt rise in second week heralds pulmonary involvement.
Normal early; falls rapidly with onset of pulmonary capillaritis/SPHS in second week.
Often normal early; falls with capillary leak, hemorrhage, or myocarditis in severe disease.
Mirrors MAP; <90 mmHg defines shock and triggers vasopressor consideration.
Often preserved or polyuric early due to non-oliguric tubular dysfunction; falls in severe disease as oliguric AKI develops.
Severe frontal/retro-orbital headache from onset; recurs with immune phase aseptic meningitis.
axes.second_peak: with immune phase aseptic meningitis around day 8–14

axes.shape_free_text: Severe diffuse myalgia with characteristic gastrocnemius (calf) tenderness, a near-specific clue for leptospirosis.

Bilateral conjunctival redness without exudate or itch, due to capillary injury; appears around day 2–5 and may persist for several days; near-specific for leptospirosis among acute febrile illnesses.
Scleral and cutaneous icterus, often greenish, in 5–10% (Weil disease); appears day 4–7 and may deepen to day 10–14 before slow resolution.
Frank hemoptysis appears late and is ominous; alveolar hemorrhage on imaging often precedes overt blood expectoration.
Petechiae on conjunctiva, palate, trunk; may evolve to ecchymoses in severe thrombocytopenia.
Mucosal, gastrointestinal, and pulmonary bleeding correlated with platelet nadir and endothelial injury.
Transient maculopapular or pretibial rash possible; not as prominent as in dengue or scrub typhus.
Mild tender hepatomegaly in roughly a quarter of severe cases; splenomegaly less common.
Confusion or obtundation due to aseptic meningitis, uremia, hyperammonemia, hypoxemia, or sepsis.
Lymphocyte-predominant CSF pleocytosis (often 10–500/μL), mildly elevated protein, and normal-to-low glucose appearing in immune phase. Many patients have asymptomatic CSF abnormalities.
Neutrophilic leukocytosis with left shift typical (often 12–25); helps distinguish from dengue and viral hepatitis. May be normal in mild disease.
Bandemia 0.05–0.20 in severe leptospiremic phase.
Falls in second half of first week; nadir often 30–100×10^9/L; lower in severe disease and predictive of bleeding/SPHS.
Falls with hemorrhage, hemolysis (rare), and dilution from resuscitation; severe anemia accompanies SPHS.
Marked acute-phase response, typically >100 mg/L in leptospiremic phase; gradual decline with effective therapy.
Often markedly elevated (>2 ng/mL); helps separate from viral mimics like dengue.
Elevated; nonspecific support for inflammation.
Often >5 mg/dL in Weil disease, may reach 20–40 mg/dL; conjugated-predominant; resolves over weeks.
Conjugated fraction comprises majority of total bilirubin (often >70%) — characteristic cholestatic signature.
Mild–moderate rise (usually 50–200 U/L), rarely >500. Disproportionately small versus bilirubin elevation, distinguishing from viral hepatitis.
Modest rise; can be amplified by rhabdomyolysis-derived AST.
Mildly elevated cholestatic pattern.
Often 5–50× upper normal in early phase from skeletal muscle injury (calves); supports differential against viral hepatitis when bilirubin and ALT are both elevated.
Rises from day 4–7; peak in second week; severe cases 4–10 mg/dL with dialysis need; recovery typical with support.
Rises in parallel with creatinine; often disproportionately high with volume depletion or GI bleeding.
Hypokalemia (often 2.5–3.5 mmol/L) early due to distal tubular kaliuresis — characteristic feature; may reverse to hyperkalemia once oliguric AKI is established.
axes.second_peak: hyperkalemia >5.5 mmol/L possible in late oliguric AKI

axes.shape_free_text: Mild hyponatremia common from SIADH-like response or volume depletion.
Falls with metabolic acidosis from AKI, lactic acidosis, or pigment nephropathy.
Elevated with shock, pulmonary hemorrhage hypoperfusion, or hepatic dysfunction.
Usually only mildly prolonged unless overt DIC or severe hepatic dysfunction; helpful to differentiate from fulminant viral hepatitis (where INR is markedly elevated).
Mildly prolonged in severe disease; helps assess for DIC overlap.
Often preserved or elevated as acute-phase reactant — helps distinguish leptospiral thrombocytopenia from overt DIC.
Elevated nonspecifically; very high values raise concern for DIC overlay.
Mild–moderate elevation in myocarditis; level correlates with poor prognosis.
Falls with capillary leak and acute illness.
Mild–moderate proteinuria from tubulointerstitial injury; rarely nephrotic-range.
Granular/muddy-brown casts, leukocyturia, microscopic hematuria reflect tubulointerstitial nephritis.
Bilateral patchy alveolar opacities reflecting alveolar hemorrhage rather than bacterial pneumonia; rapid progression typical of SPHS.
Highest sensitivity in first 7 days of illness; falls steeply thereafter.
Rises in second week and may persist for weeks.
ELISA IgM detectable from approximately day 5–7; sensitivity rises into second week.
Microscopic agglutination test (MAT) is the serologic reference standard; fourfold rise in paired sera or single titer ≥1:800 in compatible illness is diagnostic; titer typically rises after day 7.
Specific but slow (weeks to grow on EMJH medium); low sensitivity; rarely affects acute management.
Probability that the patient meets Weil syndrome criteria (jaundice + AKI + hemorrhage); rises in second week of severe disease.
Probability of meeting SPHS criteria (hypoxemia + bilateral alveolar opacities ± hemoptysis); rises sharply once pulmonary capillaritis begins.
Daily hazard for transitioning to KDIGO stage 2/3 AKI; peaks in second week.
Daily hazard for SPHS onset; peaks in second week, mortality >50% if established.
Independent ARDS development driven by alveolar hemorrhage and inflammation.
Daily hazard of clinical myocarditis with arrhythmia or cardiogenic shock.
Hazard of distributive/cardiogenic shock requiring vasopressors.
Rare but reported in severe thrombocytopenia or DIC.
ICU-acquired pneumonia, line infection, etc., particularly in mechanically ventilated SPHS patients.
Combined daily mortality hazard, peaking in second week with SPHS, severe AKI, jaundice, and shock; overall case-fatality 5–20% (severe), >50% in established SPHS.
Probability that current regimen is active against Leptospira; doxycycline/penicillin/ceftriaxone/azithromycin are all reliably active.
Rises with declining GFR; affects penicillin, cephalosporin, and supportive drug dosing.
Patient-level modifier limiting penicillin/ceftriaxone use and shifting to doxycycline/azithromycin.
Pregnancy contraindicates doxycycline (dental staining, 2nd–3rd trimester); shifts choice to penicillin G/ceftriaxone/azithromycin.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Both Weil hepatic and renal injuries arise from a shared severity axis (endothelial + organ tropism); jointly elevated values define Weil syndrome and predict mortality.
Platelet nadir is one of the strongest bedside predictors of imminent SPHS and mortality.
Falling SpO2 with rising RR often precedes overt hemoptysis by hours; early sign requiring urgent escalation.
Onset of SPHS frequently precipitates concurrent shock from hypoxemia, hemorrhage, and cytokine storm.

axis_couplings.conditionality: as oliguric AKI supervenes, hypokalemia of early phase reverses to hyperkalemia
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Phase-dependent reversal: tubular kaliuresis dominates early non-oliguric AKI (hypokalemia), then potassium accumulates with falling urine output (hyperkalemia).
Pigment nephropathy from rhabdomyolysis amplifies the tubulointerstitial AKI substrate.
AST is partly skeletal-muscle derived; co-rise with CK is a useful clue that hepatic transaminase elevation is at least partly muscle-origin in leptospirosis.
Diagnostic window: PCR sensitive in week 1, IgM and MAT take over in week 2 — they should be ordered together to maximize coverage.
Weil syndrome label captures the joint severity that drives most non-pulmonary mortality.
Established SPHS carries case-fatality often >50%; dominant pulmonary contribution to mortality in modern series.
Biphasic structure: bacteremic peak triggers and is followed by the immune-phase response, defining the clinical biphasic pattern.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Doxycycline contraindicated in pregnancy (dental staining/teratogenicity); shift to penicillin G or ceftriaxone.
Oral doxycycline alone is inadequate for SPHS or established Weil disease; IV penicillin/ceftriaxone preferred.
Severe disease warrants IV therapy.

failure_modes: delayed initiation past day 7 limits clinical benefit
underestimated severity (oral therapy chosen for occult SPHS)
treatments.context_specific_role: Mild–moderate outpatient leptospirosis and post-exposure prophylaxis (200 mg weekly for high-risk exposure).

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: History of anaphylaxis or severe cutaneous reaction precludes penicillin; substitute doxycycline (if non-pregnant) or azithromycin.
Reduce dose with falling GFR to avoid neurotoxicity (myoclonus, seizures) particularly at high doses.

failure_modes: Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction misinterpreted as worsening disease and antibiotic stopped
inadequate dosing in critically ill patient
treatments.context_specific_role: Severe/hospitalized leptospirosis (Weil disease, SPHS); historic standard.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Severe penicillin allergy with anaphylaxis cross-reactivity concern; alternative is doxycycline or azithromycin.
When clinical picture overlaps with rickettsial disease, scrub typhus, dengue with bacterial superinfection, ceftriaxone provides broader coverage while leptospirosis is clarified.

failure_modes: biliary sludging on prolonged courses (mainly pediatric)
treatments.context_specific_role: Preferred empiric IV agent for hospitalized severe leptospirosis in many modern guidelines; non-inferior to penicillin G with simpler dosing and broader empiric coverage of mimics.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Useful when both penicillin and doxycycline are contraindicated.
Safe pregnancy alternative when doxycycline avoided and beta-lactams precluded.

failure_modes: less established efficacy data for severe disease than beta-lactams
QT prolongation in patients on other QT-prolonging drugs
treatments.context_specific_role: Alternative outpatient/inpatient agent when both doxycycline and beta-lactams unsuitable; especially mild–moderate leptospirosis with overlapping rickettsial differential.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Early dialysis (initiated before classical KDIGO indications, especially with rising creatinine and oliguria) reduces leptospirosis-specific mortality in randomized data.
Oliguria + jaundice + hyperkalemia is a classical trigger for early initiation.
Volume control via RRT reduces alveolar hemorrhage burden in fluid-overloaded patients.

failure_modes: hemodynamic instability with intermittent HD (CRRT preferred in shock)

side_effects.interpretation: Anticoagulation and access-site bleeding given concurrent thrombocytopenia

treatments.context_specific_role: Early renal support is the most evidence-based mortality-modifying intervention in severe leptospirosis after antibiotics; lower threshold than in many other AKIs.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Low-tidal-volume (6 mL/kg PBW), modest PEEP ventilation reduces ventilator-induced lung injury and improves oxygenation in SPHS.

failure_modes: barotrauma from excessive PEEP in fragile lung
treatments.context_specific_role: Cornerstone of SPHS/ARDS management; should be instituted early when SpO2 falls or work of breathing rises despite oxygen.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: First-line vasopressor in distributive shock to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg after volume resuscitation.

failure_modes: inadequate volume resuscitation prior to initiation
treatments.context_specific_role: Vasopressor backbone in leptospirosis-associated shock once MAP fails to respond to balanced crystalloid resuscitation.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Aggressive volume in SPHS worsens alveolar hemorrhage; titrate to perfusion endpoints with early vasopressor and RRT volume control.

failure_modes: delay in transition to vasopressor support

side_effects.interpretation: Worsened hypoxemia from volume overload in SPHS

treatments.context_specific_role: Early restoration of intravascular volume in shock or volume depletion; transition rapidly to pressors and RRT volume control once MAP/UOP targets met.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Once oliguric AKI develops, potassium replacement is hazardous and risks hyperkalemia; monitor and reverse strategy.

treatments.context_specific_role: Early non-oliguric phase with characteristic hypokalemia from distal tubular dysfunction.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Indicated for active hemorrhage or before invasive procedures, or prophylactically when platelets <10–20×10^9/L.

failure_modes: rapid consumption in ongoing endothelial injury
treatments.context_specific_role: Adjunct in active bleeding or severe SPHS with thrombocytopenia.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: For active bleeding with coagulopathy from severe hepatic dysfunction or DIC overlap.
Transfuse for symptomatic anemia or active bleeding; conservative threshold (~7 g/dL) in stable patients.

treatments.context_specific_role: Symptomatic anemia or active SPHS-related blood loss.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Limited and conflicting evidence for high-dose pulse steroids in SPHS; some series suggest mortality reduction, others none. Used as rescue when alveolar hemorrhage is progressing despite antibiotics and ventilation.
Should be combined with appropriate antibiotic to avoid worsening unchecked infection.

failure_modes: no clear benefit in mild–moderate disease

side_effects.interpretation: Increased ICU-acquired infection risk with high-dose steroids

treatments.context_specific_role: Rescue option for severe pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome unresponsive to standard care; evidence remains controversial and should not delay antibiotics or RRT.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: VV-ECMO has been used as rescue in refractory SPHS with severe hypoxemia despite optimized ventilation.
Anticoagulation requirement complicated by ongoing alveolar hemorrhage; specialized centers, low-anticoagulation protocols.

failure_modes: circuit and mucosal bleeding from anticoagulation
delayed referral past point of irreversible damage
treatments.context_specific_role: Salvage therapy in refractory SPHS at specialized centers.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Doxycycline contraindicated in pregnancy.

failure_modes: no benefit if exposure already remote
false reassurance leading to delayed presentation
treatments.context_specific_role: 200 mg PO weekly during high-risk exposure (military deployment, flooding, eco-tourism in endemic areas) reduces clinical disease incidence.

high_exposure_farmer_sewer_slaughterhous.trajectory_modulation: earlier presentation; broader serovar exposure; risk of repeat exposure

triathlon_kayaking_swimming_in_endemic_f.trajectory_modulation: outbreak pattern with shared exposure point; younger, healthier hosts; classic skin abrasion entry

flood_or_natural_disaster_exposure_in_en.trajectory_modulation: outbreak setting; classic urban leptospirosis with rodent reservoirs

older_adult.trajectory_modulation: higher risk of severe disease (Weil, SPHS) and mortality; greater renal injury given decreased reserve

chronic_heavy_use.trajectory_modulation: amplifies hepatic injury and bleeding risk; more severe Weil presentation

diabetic.trajectory_modulation: increased AKI severity and secondary infection risk

pregnant.trajectory_modulation: severe disease risk to mother; high fetal loss with severe maternal disease; doxycycline avoided

treatment_after_day_5_of_illness.trajectory_modulation: reduced effect on bacteremia trajectory; greater accumulated organ damage; higher mortality

supportive_care: Strict input/output and daily weight monitoring; balance restoration of intravascular volume against worsening alveolar hemorrhage in SPHS — favor early vasopressor and RRT-based volume control over aggressive crystalloid loading.

Daily monitoring of creatinine, BUN, potassium, bicarbonate, lactate, and urine output; low threshold for early renal replacement therapy in oliguric AKI, hyperkalemia, severe acidosis, fluid overload, or rising azotemia.
Replace potassium and magnesium aggressively in early non-oliguric phase, but reverse strategy (anticipate hyperkalemia) once urine output falls.
Avoid nephrotoxic and nephroactive agents: NSAIDs, aminoglycosides if avoidable, IV contrast unless essential.
Continuous SpO2 and respiratory rate monitoring; intubate early when tachypnea, declining SpO2, or hemoptysis appear — do not wait for classic ARDS thresholds in SPHS.

Lung-protective ventilation (Vt 6 mL/kg PBW, plateau pressure ≤30 cmH2O), conservative fluid balance once shock corrected, prone positioning in refractory hypoxemia, ECMO referral in salvage candidates.

Continuous cardiac monitoring for arrhythmia and conduction disturbance in suspected myocarditis; troponin and ECG on admission and with clinical change; echocardiogram if hypotension persists despite filling.
Anticipate and recognize Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction in the first hours after antibiotic initiation; treat with antipyretics, fluids, and supportive care without stopping antibiotics.
Monitor platelet count and coagulation daily; platelet/FFP/RBC transfusion guided by bleeding rather than fixed thresholds; avoid anticoagulation during active SPHS where possible.
Lumbar puncture if aseptic meningitis suspected in immune phase, after correcting platelet count and coagulopathy; supportive analgesia for headache.
Eye exam in convalescence — late uveitis (weeks to months after acute illness) is a recognized sequela needing ophthalmology referral.
Public-health notification: leptospirosis is a notifiable disease in many jurisdictions; report to relevant authorities and review exposure source for cluster investigation.

Patient and household education: avoid contaminated freshwater, use protective footwear and gloves in occupational exposures, rodent control, and consider doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis 200 mg weekly during ongoing high-risk exposure.
Send paired serology (acute + convalescent at 2–4 weeks) and PCR (blood early, urine in second week) before assuming disease excluded; negative day-1 IgM does not rule out leptospirosis.
Multidisciplinary involvement: nephrology for early RRT, intensivist for SPHS, infectious diseases for diagnostic confirmation and antimicrobial stewardship, obstetrics for pregnant patients.

Discharge planning includes follow-up creatinine, liver enzymes, complete blood count, ophthalmology review, and counseling regarding fatigue and possible post-leptospirosis syndrome lasting weeks to months.
